beats.narration_text: Someone assumed Claude approves a trademark for legal use. Wrong — it screens the proposed name against a fixed checklist and reports the matches. Here's what actually runs when you invoke it.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. A Skill is a folder on disk — this one's called clearance. Inside sits one file, SKILL.md, written in plain English. No branching, no compiled logic. Claude reads it, then acts. They chose auditability over cleverness: the file is the program.

props.title: A skill is a folder.
props.calloutText: The SKILL.md is the instruction set.

beats.narration_text: The mechanism is deliberately simple. Instructions live under a heading called Steps. Claude reads step one, executes it, moves to step two — top to bottom, no branching unless a step itself says otherwise. Every action traces back to a line you can point at.

One constraint is worth pulling apart. Screen the proposed name against the sources and criteria the file names, then flag anything that matches. That's the whole job. They optimized for a report that holds its shape every time at the expense of judgement calls — the model isn't asked whether a hit is fatal, only whether it exists.

props.heading: The interesting constraint.
props.body: Screen the proposed name against the checklist; flag matches — not verdicts.

beats.narration_text: Same checklist in, same report out, every time. Whether the mark is actually clear to use — that call is still yours.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I'm about to publish a new product under a name I want to protect. Before I file or announce anything, walk me through what a preliminary trademark clearance screen actually checks — federal register, common-law usage, domain and social handles, foreign filings — how you'd rank the risk of a partial match, what evidence pushes a hit from noise to stop-shipping-and-get-a-lawyer, and what a clearance report should contain so a real trademark attorney could act on it in one pass. Then ask me your first question. Go deeper: what changes if I'm launching in the EU or Japan instead of the US — where does the search shift, and which classes get harder to clear?

llm_exercise.prompt: I'm about to publish a new product under a name I want to protect. Before I file or announce anything, walk me through: (1) what a preliminary trademark clearance screen actually checks — federal register, common-law usage, domain and social handles, foreign filings — and what each source can and can't tell me; (2) how you'd rank the risk of a partial match (same class vs adjacent class, phonetic vs visual similarity); (3) what evidence would push a hit from noise to stop-shipping-and-get-a-lawyer; and (4) what a clearance report should contain so a real trademark attorney could act on it in one pass. Then ask me your first question.
